lesson.title: Monotonicity: Stitching Increasing and Decreasing Into One Map
lesson.summary: Monotonicity describes whether a function is increasing, decreasing, or neither on a given stretch of its domain, and for a differentiable function that behavior can only switch at a critical number, which is what makes a single sign chart of f prime a complete map of the function's shape.
lesson.body:
A function is called monotonic on an interval if it is either entirely increasing or entirely decreasing throughout that interval, with no mixing of the two. A function can be monotonic on one piece of its domain and behave the opposite way on another piece, the way f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 increases, then decreases, then increases again. What makes monotonicity a genuinely useful organizing idea is a fact guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem: if f is differentiable on an interval, the only places its monotonicity can switch from increasing to decreasing or back are at critical numbers, points where f'(x) = 0 or f' fails to exist. Between any two consecutive critical numbers, f' cannot change sign, so it is either always positive or always negative on that whole stretch.

That fact turns finding all the monotonic intervals of a function into a short procedure: find every critical number, use those numbers to cut the domain into pieces, then test one point in each piece. For f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5, the derivative f'(x) = 3(x - 3)(x + 1) has critical numbers x = -1 and x = 3, giving three pieces. Testing x = -2, x = 0, and x = 4 in f' gives signs positive, negative, positive, respectively, as shown in the increasing and decreasing sections above. Laid out as a single monotonicity table: on (negative infinity, -1) the sign of f' is positive and f is increasing; on (-1, 3) the sign of f' is negative and f is decreasing; on (3, positive infinity) the sign of f' is positive again and f is increasing. Reading straight across that table gives the complete monotonic structure of f in one glance, and every place the behavior flips, x = -1 and x = 3, is a local extremum.

Not every function alternates like this. Some functions are monotonic across their entire domain: f(x) = e^x has derivative f'(x) = e^x, which is positive for every real x, so e^x is increasing everywhere and never has a local max or min to speak of. Similarly f(x) = -x^3 has derivative -3x^2, which is negative or zero everywhere, so that function is decreasing across its whole domain. The cubic used throughout this chapter is more typical of what you will see in practice: a mix of increasing and decreasing pieces stitched together at critical numbers, and reading that mix off a single sign chart is the core skill this section builds toward.
